newsitem.title: USA: Dole wants ban on campaign money from non-citizens.
newsitem.headline: Dole wants ban on campaign money from non-citizens.

text.p: Charging that foreign interests were trying to buy White House access through big-bucks donations to the Democratic party, Republican Bob Dole on Sunday called for banning all campaign contributions from non-citizens.

In a hard-hitting speech advocating a major overhaul of campaign finance laws, the Republican presidential nominee also took on the AFL-CIO, which is bankrolling a $35 million campaign to elect Democrats to Congress, saying it was time to stop use of compulsory union dues for political purposes.

The Democratic National Committee (DNC) is under fire for accepting questionable campaign contributions from individuals with ties to the Lippo Group, an Indonesian real estate and banking conglomerate.

DNC officials on Friday removed fundraiser John Huang, who formerly worked for the Lippo Group, and asked the Federal Election Commission to investigate charges regarding some of the donations he brought in. Democrats have also been criticised for a recent fundraiser held at a Buddhist temple in California.

"Foreign aid has finally reached America. It's reaching the United States now, it's all going to the Democratic National Committee," Dole said, charging foreign contributors were trying to buy access to the White House.

"We simply cannot allow the influence of any American to be outweighed by foreign money ... if you're not eligible to vote, you shouldn't be allowed to contribute to politicians in America," Dole said.

Dole said if elected he would create a bipartisan commission to recommend an overhaul of campaign finance reform laws including abolishing so-called "soft money" -- contributions to political parties to get around strict limits on giving to individual candidates.
He also made a vague promise to rein in the influence of political action committees.
President Bill Clinton's re-election campaign responded "It's a little late and disingenuous for Bob Dole to promote campaign finance reform.
"Bob Dole has made a career opposing meaningful campaign finance reform," said spokesman Joe Lockhart. "It's too bad that Senator Bob Dole's record doesn't match candidate Dole's rhetoric."
Promises to overhaul finance laws are a staple of political campaigns but have produced few concrete results in recent years.

Clinton and House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, appearing together in New Hampshire in 1995, recommended the type of bipartisan panel Dole is suggesting. But campaign finance reform died in Congress and both parties have stepped up fundraising.
Dole's call for a bipartisan commission appeared to be a partisan political jab at Clinton, reflecting his strategy of attacking the ethics of his opponent.

"It will be your election and not the election of some foreign interest or special interest that you have no control over," Dole said, saying massive reform was needed to renew Americans' faith in the political system.

But the fact that Dole decided to make a trip to this rock-ribbed Republican state only 16 days before the election reflects the problems he is facing. Dole trails Clinton, who narrowly won the state in 1992, by double-digits here and the president may sweep the Northeast.
Dole is not the only Republican in trouble here. New Hampshire Republican Sen. Bob Smith is locked in a tight race, helping fuel Democrts' hopes they may retake the Senate this year.

Dole has never received a friendly welcome in New Hampshire -- he lost the state's pivotal primary -- and Sunday was no exception. Dole's campaign plane landed in the midst of a raging storm that tossed it back and forth so hard overhead panels opened, releasing emergency oxygen bags.
Monday and Tuesday Dole will visit Michigan, another must- win state where he lags in the polls.
